title: Inverter-based OTA
description: A complementary common-source (inverter) transconductor: an NMOS and a PMOS input device stacked between the rails share the same bias current, and their gates tie together as the input. Because both devices transconduct the input, the composite transconductance is the sum $g_{m,tot} = g_{m,n} + g_{m,p}$ — current reuse buys roughly double the $g_m$ for the same current, so the effective $g_m/I_D$ is $(g_m/I_D)_n + (g_m/I_D)_p$. Gain is $g_{m,tot}/(g_{ds,n} + g_{ds,p})$ and, for the same current, the input-referred thermal density is about $\sqrt{2}$ lower than a single device. The cost is supply sensitivity: the bias current and hence $g_m$ depend directly on VDD, so the inverter needs a replica or common-mode bias loop and has poor native PSRR — sim owns the supply rejection. The PMOS device takes a sign param like the mirror-load convention so it binds against either an N-style or a signed-PMOS table.

params.name: vn_target
params.note: input-referred thermal density budget (the current-reuse benefit should beat a single device)

params.name: V_out_dc
params.note: output DC level (mid-supply for symmetric swing); sets both devices' vds

params.name: sign_p
params.note: vds sign convention of the PMOS table: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis

params.name: I_bias
params.note: the single current shared by the N and P devices (current reuse)

params.name: gm_id_n
params.note: NMOS inversion: its share of the composite transconductance and noise

params.name: gm_id_p
params.note: PMOS inversion: its share of the composite transconductance and noise

doc.title: NMOS input device
doc.description: The common-source NMOS half of the inverter; its source at ground, drain at the output DC level.

doc.title: PMOS input device
doc.description: The common-source PMOS half of the inverter; its source at VDD, drain at the output DC level. Shares the NMOS bias current (current reuse).

rows.name: gm_tot
rows.note: current reuse: both devices transconduct the input, so their gm add

rows.name: gm_id_eff
rows.note: effective composite gm/ID = gm_id_n + gm_id_p — the current-reuse efficiency win

rows.name: Rout
rows.note: the resistance this stage presents at its output — both devices' output conductances in parallel. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this row is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

rows.name: Av
rows.note: composite transconductance into the two output conductances in parallel

rows.name: vn_in
rows.note: each device's own drain-noise density summed in current and referred by gm_tot; ~sqrt(2) below a single device at the same current

rows.name: vos
rows.expr: sqrt(pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, n__W, L_n, gm_id_n)^2 + pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, p__W, L_p, gm_id_p)^2)
rows.note: estimate: the N and P threshold-mismatch offsets combined, input-referred

rows.name: cgg_in
rows.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents. Both gates are driven together, so both gate capacitances load the driver. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it — and here the drain swings against the gate, so that omission is at its worst. No rule reads it

rules.note: computed from the gamma-model floor; this table carries no measured noise; the simulator owns noise sign-off
the stacked N and P must both stay saturated between the rails with a little margin
estimate: very high composite gm/ID means weak inversion and strong VDD dependence of the bias — budget a common-mode bias loop; sim owns PSRR
